finding: §2 says the recommendation for the changed branch 'is decided here rather than left to an implementer', then decides a string for a branch it does not name. The trigger it names is 'the first clean round of a streak that still holds warning/info rows' — at audit_clean_rounds: 2 that round is not converged — but the text it decides ('states that the phase may proceed') is the converged branch's, and §7 row 10 pins only 'a converged round holding non-PASS rows'. Audit next_action has three branches (converged / open rows / clean-but-not-yet-converged); the branch §2 actually names ends the release with no decided text and no test row, so the implementer must invent the one sentence §2 says exists to stop an operator learning silently that a round closed over open rows.
suggestion: Give the exact recommendation for each of the two affected branches — clean-but-not-converged with non-PASS rows, and converged with non-PASS rows — and add a §7 row for the first.

finding: §3 calls the uncovering refusal 'an escalation rather than a deadlock' because 'the operator's resolution is to write the field explicitly into the imported document', but under the change rule that remedy works for only one of the two literals and §3 names neither. Writing `all` makes resolved-after equal resolved-before and passes — at the cost of the project-level `blocking` the operator deliberately set. Writing `blocking` changes the resolved value away from the task-level `all` and is refused by exactly the rule §3 states, and refused again on every retry, because the task override that would make resolved-before `blocking` is never written. So the stated resolution either abandons the field or does not lift the refusal, and an implementer cannot tell which import the fence is supposed to permit.
suggestion: Name the literal the operator writes and what happens on the retry. If an explicit `blocking` must be admitted once, state the mechanism (an attended import, an approved escalation, or a first-write exemption) instead of letting 'write the field explicitly' carry it.

finding: §3's new escalation paragraph rests on a ground the tree falsifies: "This is what separates it from the two deadlocks in the table, where *every* import was refused and no document the unit could write would pass." For the uncovering import, two documents the unit CAN write pass, and neither needs a human. (1) Omit the top-level `workflow` key: internal/cli/importcmd.go:158 preserves the existing task-level block whenever `importedHasWorkflowKey(trimmed)` is false (internal/cli/import_workflow.go:11-22 keys on the raw top-level key), so the task-level `all` survives, resolved-before equals resolved-after, and the change rule passes. (2) Carry `"audit_converge_on": "all"` in the document's workflow block: §3 says "a write of `all` never trips it". So the refusal is a correctable authoring error the unit can fix in one edit, not a decision reserved for the operator — and escalating it stops the entire run (stop_reason: escalation) for something the unit already had the means to fix. §3 tells the unit neither remedy, and §7 holds no row asserting a passing document exists.
suggestion: Replace the escalation claim with the true one: the refusal is answerable by the unit — re-emit the document without a top-level `workflow` key, or with `audit_converge_on` set to the value that already resolves — and reserve `tp escalate --decision audit-converge-on` for a unit that intends the relax. Add a §7 row asserting that both of those documents import cleanly under TP_UNATTENDED=1 over a task-level `all` and a project-level `blocking`, with the mutant 'refuse any import while the two layers disagree'.

finding: §6a declares its five-item list exhaustive -- "The list is exhaustive over what `git grep` finds today; a sixth would be a defect in this section" -- and §2 of this same file names the sixth and seventh four paragraphs earlier. §2: "Both audit sinks compute `next_action` from the round's `clean`, each carrying a comment asserting the equivalence this release breaks -- that a round's non-`PASS` rows are exactly `!clean`." Those two comments are shipped and I read them: internal/cli/audit_record.go:124 ("The just-recorded round is the latest, so its non-PASS rows are exactly !clean.") and internal/cli/audit_record.go:389 ("The latest recorded round holding open non-PASS rows is exactly !Clean."). Neither is in §6a's five, and no §7 row reverses either. Two more, both in artifacts §6a already names and so not reachable by a fresh `git grep` for a new file: (a) skills/tp/SKILL.md:149 is ONE sentence, and §6a.2 names only its "counts every non-PASS row" clause -- the same sentence continues "the stored per-round `clean` flag, `next_action` and the `--status --check` exit code are unchanged" and ends "so `--check` still exits 1 and `next_action` still reads fix-and-re-audit", every clause of which §2 falsifies; (b) skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:883-885 ("Whenever `divergence` is emitted over state tp itself recorded, `next_action` reads the fix-and-re-audit directive") is a DIFFERENT paragraph from the "Honest Convergence Signals" paragraph §6a.4 names at 753-756, and is falsified by the case §6a.5's own repair does not cover: under `blocking` a round that is clean but not yet converged satisfies all five divergence conditions while both sinks pass `latestRoundHasFindings = !clean = false`, so the object is emitted beside branch 3, not branch 2. The count is therefore at least seven by the spec's own text, and §6a's stated standard is that a sixth is a defect in the section.
suggestion: Re-derive the list from the call graph out of the stored `clean` flag rather than from a grep, and state the count as whatever that walk returns. Add at minimum: internal/cli/audit_record.go:124 and :389 (the two comments §2 already names); the remainder of skills/tp/SKILL.md:149, edited as a whole sentence rather than as the "counts every non-PASS row" clause; and skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:883-885. Give each a §7 row. Then either drop the exhaustiveness sentence or bind it to a named artifact -- "the list is exactly the sites the walk in <task> enumerates" -- so it cannot rot the way this one did in the round that wrote it.

finding: §6a stakes exhaustiveness and is falsified by the cheapest possible grep, which is the method §6a itself declares insufficient. It says the list 'is exhaustive over what `git grep` finds today; a sixth would be a defect in this section' and explains that the two additions 'were found by walking the call graph out of `clean` rather than by searching for the sentence, which is why searching had missed them'. Run this session: `git grep -n review_converge_on -- skills/ README.md` returns 6 hits, and three are shipped assertions this release falsifies or invalidates that are in none of the five. (a) `skills/tp/SKILL.md:153` — 'tp has no audit-side equivalent of `review_converge_on` yet.' This release is that equivalent; the sentence is not §6a item 2, which is the different sentence at SKILL.md:149 in the `divergence` block. (b) `skills/tp/SKILL.md:269` — the `tp set --workflow` field table enumerates every settable workflow field and omits `audit_converge_on`. (c) `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:478` — the workflow-field table has a `review_converge_on` row and no `audit_converge_on` row. A fourth, adjacent instance: §6a item 2 characterises SKILL.md:149 as 'saying audit convergence counts every non-`PASS` row', but that sentence asserts three things unchanged — 'the stored per-round `clean` flag, `next_action` and the `--status --check` exit code' — which is exactly the over-promise §6a item 4 flags in REFERENCE.md's parallel paragraph. §7 row 19 pins only the counting clause, so the SKILL.md over-promise ships false with the guard green. The AX cost is the count itself: L266-269 is 571 bytes of self-defence ('The count has been one, two, three and is now five, and each rise came from someone counting rather than reasoning'), the number has now been wrong at 1, 2, 3 and 5, it has consumed a finding in four separate rounds, and it is wrong again.
suggestion: Delete L266-269 entirely. Replace the count with the derivation a check can run: 'every sentence in `skills/`, `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` that a `git grep -n "review_converge_on\|audit convergence\|non-PASS" -- skills/ README.md CLAUDE.md` reaches, plus every doc comment on the call graph out of `clean`.' Then §7 gets one row asserting that grep returns no sentence stating a rule false under either value of the field, instead of rows 19 and 20 naming two sentences by hand. A rule cannot be short by one; a number has been four times.

finding: §6a's title and item 1 say the gate guard's assertion is *reversed*; row 18 says the call sites "become nine". These predict different test files and cannot both be written. Verified by reading internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:469-503: TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate holds exactly eleven `assert.`/`require.` call sites (473, 474, 481, 484, 485, 490, 493, 494, 497, 498, 500), of which exactly two (473, 474) name `audit_converge_on`, and two of the remaining nine are `require.True(t, ok)` decode checks — so §6a.1's counting rule verifies. But a *reversed* assertion still occupies its call site (it now asserts the write succeeds), which leaves eleven, not nine; only a *deleted* assertion leaves nine. Row 18 additionally cannot fail its own mutant: if the two are deleted, the nine survivors are precisely "the ones that do not name `audit_converge_on`", so "delete the surrounding block" satisfies the assertion verbatim.
suggestion: Decide and state it once: either the two sites are replaced in place (then the row asserts eleven call sites of which two assert that `audit_converge_on=blocking` is accepted at exit 0) or they are removed (then the row must additionally assert where the positive assertion now lives, which is what makes deletion distinguishable from repair).

finding: §6a.5 and §2 both assert that no line of engine/divergence.go changes, and §6a.3 -- three items above it in the same list -- requires editing a line of that exact file. §6a.5: "suppression is correct and the release changes no line of `divergence.go`." §2 line 100: "No line of `engine/divergence.go` changes; what changes is the doc comment calling that condition redundant, which §6a.5 takes." But `engine.DivergenceHint` is declared at internal/engine/divergence.go:16-19 -- a `const`, executable code emitted verbatim as `divergence.hint`, not a comment -- and §6a.3 requires its final clause to be rewritten. The claim is false a second time on its own terms: the `ComputeAuditDivergence` doc comment §6a.5 itself edits is internal/engine/divergence.go:101-109, so the sentence "the release changes no line of `divergence.go`. What it changes is a comment" contradicts itself, since that comment IS a line of divergence.go. The sentence matters because it is the sizing signal a decomposer reads: taken literally it says divergence.go is out of scope, while the release must edit two separate places in it, one of them shipped code whose change propagates to internal/engine/divergence_test.go:166 and :176 and to internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go:145 (which asserts REFERENCE.md contains the constant verbatim, so REFERENCE.md:879 must be edited in the same commit or the guard reddens).
suggestion: Replace both sentences with what is actually meant and make the scope explicit: "No line of `ComputeAuditDivergence`'s BODY changes -- the suppression is already correct. Two other places in `engine/divergence.go` do change: the `DivergenceHint` constant (§6a.3) and the condition-4 doc comment (§6a.5), and because `internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go` asserts `REFERENCE.md` contains the constant verbatim, `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`:879 changes in the same commit." Say "no behaviour changes" wherever "no line changes" is meant.

finding: §6a.5 asserts "the behaviour is already right" on an argument that covers severity and not attribution, and the population it misses is measured, non-empty, and 100% inside the class `blocking` makes invisible. The argument: divergence "hands the driver a decision about whether open findings should gate a release" and under `blocking` "that is exactly the state an operator has chosen, so suppression is correct." But divergence's third message form asks a different question, and it is one no operator answered by setting a severity policy: engine/divergence.go:130-132 and :187-190 count rows carrying NO role into `unattributed_open` and render "none attributed to a role (possibly spec-coverage's)" -- i.e. the warning that the spec-coverage streak this repository ships on may be understated because some open rows could be spec-coverage's. That is a caveat about the RELIABILITY of the conformance measurement, not about whether advisory findings gate. Nothing else in the payload carries it: engine/rolestreaks.go:132-134 (`auditRoundOpenByRole`) skips roleless rows outright, so `role_streaks[].open` cannot express them; §4's `by_severity` keys on severity; §2's new `next_action` carries only an aggregate count. Measured this session over all 90 recorded audit-round files (10,435 rows, 360 non-PASS): 20 non-PASS rows carry no role, and their severities are `warning` 11 / `info` 9 -- ZERO `error`. So in tp's entire recorded audit history every roleless open row is non-blocking under `blocking`, makes its round clean, and after `audit_clean_rounds` such rounds sets `converged`, which is condition 4 -- suppressing the only field that counts them. §2's own framing ("divergence exists to ask whether open findings should gate a release and the operator has already answered") is what hides this: the operator answered the severity question, and the attribution question is silently answered for them at the moment of the ship decision. §6a.5 also generalises from the wrong side of the fixture -- the case it reasons about is a round whose open rows are attributed, which is the only case a reader of the section constructs.
suggestion: Either (a) state in §2 and §6a.5 that `unattributed_open` disappears from the payload once a `blocking` round converges, name that as an accepted loss, and say where the operator reads it instead -- the honest answer today is nowhere, so this needs a surface; or (b) make condition 4 severity-aware in one direction only: suppress on a converged round whose open non-PASS rows all carry a role, and keep emitting when `unattributed_open > 0`, which is exactly the state where a decision does remain. Whichever is chosen, add a §7 row with the mutant "suppress on every converged round, which drops the 20-row roleless population measured in spec/.tp-review", and drop "the behaviour is already right" unless (a) is taken.

finding: Row 14's column-4 cell states in its own words that the named mutant satisfies the row's assertion. The assertion is "a fenced refusal records `--decision audit-converge-on` and its message names this field"; the mutant is "reuse the command-field message, which interpolates the field name and so satisfies a substring check". Verified against the tree: internal/cli/unattended.go's refuseUnattendedCommandField formats "%s names a command the driver executes and cannot be set under TP_UNATTENDED, at any layer" with the field interpolated, so reusing it produces a message containing `audit_converge_on` and passes any check the row as written can support. The column was renamed to "the mutant that must fail it", and this cell holds a mutant the row provably cannot fail.
suggestion: State the discriminating observable rather than the trap: pin what the message must contain that the command-field message cannot — e.g. the message must name the field AND the value that was refused AND must not contain the command-field clause 'names a command the driver executes'. Alternatively pin the new message's literal shape the way §3 pins the enum name.

finding: A quarter of the spec is the review loop's own drafting history, and it is not the knob that grew. Counted this session: 7,044 of 29,155 bytes (24.2%) and 81 of 353 lines sit in nine paragraph spans whose subject is a rejected draft, a superseded count, or a round postmortem — L3-16 (1,203 B, the round-7 postmortem blockquote), L53-58 (598 B, 'An earlier draft wrote `all` as...' including 'It was written while deleting the word *surviving* for imprecision'), L64-66 (235 B, 'because two earlier drafts left it to be inferred and both inferred it wrong'), L100-103 (375 B, 'the call graph out of `clean` is what found it'), L156-170 (1,289 B, §3's three rejected rules), L210-222 (1,170 B, §4's reverted draft and the dependency it no longer has), L236-244 (726 B, §5), L263-269 (571 B, §6a's count history), L308-317 (877 B, §7's round-9/10 postmortem). None of it is a decision to build; all of it is re-read by every role of every future round and by the decomposer. The load-bearing half of this finding is the control: the knob itself is NOT bloated. §2+§2.1 is 7,578 bytes; the same ground in the shipped twin — spec/0.31.0.md §3.3-3.5 (field, resolution, validation, exit-code split, recompute policy) plus §4 (blocking set, unknown severity is blocking) — is 8,248 bytes, so the audit knob's own sections are 8% SMALLER than the review knob's. Every byte of growth is in sections the loop wrote about itself: §7 is now 7,206 bytes (24.7% of the file) and has overtaken §2+§2.1, the decisions it derives from. Round 10 to round 11 alone added 13,674 bytes and removed 7,204 (snapshots 22,685 to 29,155).
suggestion: Cut, in order of bytes returned: L3-16 (the postmortem belongs in the commit that rewrote the file — the git log already carries it); L308-317 (§7's preamble: keep one sentence, 'each row names the decision it derives from and the mutant that must fail it', and drop the round-9/round-10 measurements); L210-222 (§4: keep 'Emitted when the round holds at least one non-`PASS` row; the condition is a property of the rows and nothing else' and drop the reverted-draft narrative); L236-244 (§5, see the separate finding); L263-269 (§6a's count, see the separate finding); the second half of L53-58 and all of L64-66 and L100-103 (keep the 2,913-row measurement, which is load-bearing for the wording; drop 'It was written while deleting...', 'two earlier drafts... inferred it wrong', and 'the call graph out of `clean` is what found it'). That is roughly 5,500 bytes, 19% of the file, and nothing an implementer builds is lost.

finding: This round's revert of §4's emission condition makes deliverable 3 unconditional, which falsifies deliverable 1's promise in the same list. §1 deliverable 1: "Default `all`, which is the behaviour tp ships today, so a project that does not set it sees no change." §4 as reverted: "Emitted when the round holds at least one non-`PASS` row, and it survives `--compact`. The condition is a property of the rows and nothing else." So `by_severity` appears on `tp audit --merge` for EVERY project -- including every project that never sets the field, which by deliverable 1 is every project -- and it appears in `--compact`, the mode §2.1 of spec/0.33.0.md says an agent driver runs in. Measured this session with the dev binary on a real round (spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/audit-round-4.ndjson, 200 rows, 4 non-PASS): today's `--merge` payload carries `by_role`, `by_status`, `duplicates_removed`, `findings`, `input_files`, `inputs`, `merged_count`, `output_path` and (non-compact only) `overlap_report`; `--compact` strips `overlap_report` and nothing else. `by_severity` would be a new key on both, for all projects, on a command §1 frames as buying an opt-in feature. §5 and §6 do not mention it, and §6a does not list REFERENCE.md's `tp audit --merge` output documentation among what changes -- a further instance of §6a's exhaustiveness gap. This is not an argument for reverting the revert: round 10's finding that the clean-under-policy condition emptied the buckets stands. It is that §1's "sees no change" and §4's "a property of the rows and nothing else" are now the two halves of a contradiction, and §1 is what a decomposer reads to size the release.
suggestion: Fix §1 rather than §4. Rewrite deliverable 1 to scope its promise: "Default `all`, which is the behaviour tp ships today, so a project that does not set it sees no change in what the audit gate counts." And rewrite deliverable 3 to say what §4 now decides: "the breakdown of every non-`PASS` row on `tp audit --merge`, emitted whenever there is one -- under either value of the field, so it is the one part of this release every project sees." Then name `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`'s `tp audit --merge` output section in §6a and give it a §7 row, since a new unconditional key in an agent-parsed payload is a documented-contract change.

finding: Both new paragraphs assert something the release's own §6a falsifies. §2: "No line of `engine/divergence.go` changes; what changes is the doc comment calling that condition redundant". §6a.5: "the release changes no line of `divergence.go`. What it changes is a comment". But `engine.DivergenceHint` — the shipped constant §6a.3 and §7 row 19 require to be rewritten — is DEFINED IN THAT FILE, at internal/engine/divergence.go:16-19, and the doc comment §6a.5 reverses is at lines 101-109 of the same file. So the release changes engine/divergence.go in two places, one of them executable code. A decomposer reading §2 would exclude the file from the release's edit set and then find §6a.3 demanding an edit to it.
suggestion: Say what is true: divergence.go's LOGIC is unchanged — `ComputeAuditDivergence` keeps all five conditions — while the file changes twice, at `DivergenceHint` (§6a.3) and at the doc comment (§6a.5).

finding: Three surfaces must classify a row's severity identically and the spec names a shared mechanism for none of them: record-time stamping (§2), the replay's per-round grading (row 11), and `--merge`'s buckets (row 17, whose invariant is that `error` + `unrecognised` equals the round's blocking-row count). §2 also forbids grading at read time, so the replay needs a pure grader the runtime does not otherwise expose, and §4 says the merge path has no access to the resolved policy at all. §7's own second paragraph says a row depending on a function states it; rows 5-8, 11 and 17 name none, so three independent classifications can drift while every row stays green.
suggestion: Name one predicate over (rows, resolved policy) and state that stamping, the replay and the merge buckets all derive from it, so row 17's invariant cannot drift from §2's rule.

finding: §2 decides a `next_action` recommendation neither audit sink can compute from what it passes, and §7 test 10's own mutant column shows why. §2: on a converged round holding non-`PASS` rows the recommendation "states that the phase may proceed and names how many non-`PASS` rows were accepted, so the sentence differs observably from the one an empty round produces." Read this session: `engine.AuditNextAction(specPath string, converged, latestRoundHasFindings bool)` (internal/engine/nextaction.go:76) takes two booleans and no count, and BOTH sinks pass the negation of the stored flag -- internal/cli/audit_record.go:125 passes `!clean`, and :390 passes `len(rounds) > 0 && !rounds[len(rounds)-1].Clean`. Under `blocking` a converged round holding advisory rows has `clean == true`, so both sinks pass `(converged=true, latestRoundHasFindings=false)`: the function is handed exactly the inputs an EMPTY converged round produces and cannot render a count or differ by one byte. §7 test 10's mutant is "branch on `clean` alone, which makes the two strings equal" -- but branching on `clean` alone is the shipped code, so the mutant is the current state and the row asserts a behaviour no stated change reaches. The release therefore needs a third input to `AuditNextAction` (the round's non-PASS row count), which is a signature change to a shipped exported function that §2, §3, §4 and §6a all leave unnamed -- and which reverses the enumerated three-branch doc comment at internal/engine/nextaction.go:63-75 that §6a's exhaustive list also omits.
suggestion: State the input in §2: "`AuditNextAction` gains the round's non-`PASS` row count as a third argument; both sinks already hold it (`--record` from the round it just stored, `--status` from the latest round's rows) and both currently pass only `!clean`." Add `internal/engine/nextaction.go`'s three-branch doc comment to §6a as a reversed assertion, since a converged round now has two recommendations rather than one. Rewrite test 10's mutant as "keep the two-argument signature, which hands both sinks the inputs an empty converged round produces".

finding: §2 requires next_action to name 'how many non-`PASS` rows were accepted' and row 10 requires that numeral on both audit sinks, but the population is never named. Three candidates in this same release disagree: the latest recorded round's non-`PASS` row total, the sum of `role_streaks[].open` (which §4 calls severity-blind and unconditional on both sinks), and `--merge`'s `findings`. They differ whenever a row carries no role or a role contributes no rows to the latest round, and only the second is already available to `--status` without re-reading the round file.
suggestion: Name the population — the non-`PASS` rows of the latest recorded round — and say whether it is recomputed or read from an already-emitted field, so both sinks provably print the same number.

finding: §2's "**One shipped signal reads `clean` and therefore does change: `divergence`.**" is a uniqueness claim over a set §2 itself enumerates differently two paragraphs earlier, and it is false on at least four counts. §2 line 84: "`blocking` governs `clean`, and therefore also `next_action`, which is derived from it" -- so `next_action` is a second shipped signal reading `clean`, named by §2 before the uniqueness sentence denies it. Read this session: engine/reviewstate.go:429-438 `ConsecutiveClean` walks `rounds[i].Clean`, and :509-511 `Converged` is `ConsecutiveClean >= required && !stale`, so the reported top-level `consecutive_clean`, the reported `converged`, and the exit code of `tp audit --status --check` all read the stored flag and all change value under `blocking`. `divergence` does not even read `clean` directly -- it reads `Converged` (divergence.go:120). The claim is exactly the shape CLAUDE.md names as this repository's recurring defect ("never assert a quantifier you did not count"), and here it is load-bearing rather than decorative: §6a.4's repair strikes ONE of the five items REFERENCE.md:753-756 lists as unchanged (`engine.Converged`, `engine.ConsecutiveClean`, the stored per-round `clean` flag, the `--status --check` exit code, `next_action`'s three-state precedence), leaving four standing and false, and §7 test 20 pins only that one strike. The undercount in §2 is what sized the repair in §6a.
suggestion: Delete the count. Write instead: "Everything downstream of the stored `clean` flag changes value under `blocking`: `consecutive_clean`, `converged`, the exit code of `tp audit --status --check`, `next_action` (above) and `divergence` (below). The first four are the release's intent; `divergence` is the one whose direction is not obvious, so it is stated here." Then extend §6a.4 and §7 test 20 to strike all five items from REFERENCE.md:753-756, not the `clean` flag alone.

finding: §2's new paragraph opens "**One shipped signal reads `clean` and therefore does change: `divergence`.**" and justifies itself as the place "where a reader looks for what `clean` touches", but it is an uncounted uniqueness claim and it misses the most consequential reader: the resume/run phase oracle. internal/engine/resume.go:87 computes `auditConverged := Converged(auditRounds, wf.AuditCleanRounds, specHash)` from each round's stored `Clean`, and internal/engine/phase.go's DetectPhase turns that into `PhaseRelease` (rule 3, 'tasks exist, all done, audit converged → release'); `tp run` then exits 0 with stop_reason converged. So under `blocking` the driver declares a cycle releasable while `warning`/`info` rows are open — the release's actual behavioural consequence, and it is stated nowhere. Same shape as the claims this file has already had falsified twice (a uniqueness assertion over a set nobody enumerated).
suggestion: Enumerate the readers of `clean` rather than asserting a count: `converged`/`consecutive_clean`, `next_action` (already named), `divergence`, and the resume/run oracle's phase and `tp run`'s converged exit. State explicitly that under `blocking` `tp resume`/`tp run` reach `release`/exit 0 over open advisory rows, since that is what an operator setting the knob is buying.

finding: The SKILL.md severity-mix recipe was obsoleted by the very next repair commit and left standing, so the release now ships two routes to one number and the untested one is the one §2.1 names. Commit 32765c8 ('give 0.37.0's operator the number the default decision needs') added L130-134: 'the previous cycle's mix is recoverable only by counting `severity` across its `audit-round-*.ndjson`. No flag is added for this. `skills/tp/SKILL.md` carries the one-line command that derives it.' Commit 071bc52, the next commit on this file, reverted §4's emission predicate to a property of the rows. Measured this session over the whole tracked corpus (90 `audit-round-*.ndjson` files, 10,435 rows): 70 of 90 round files (78%) carry at least one non-`PASS` row, so under the reverted predicate `by_severity` is emitted on 78% of rounds under BOTH policy values, including the default `all` the previous cycle ran under. That breakdown is exactly the previous cycle's mix. The word 'only' in L132 is now false, and the release pays for a shell one-liner that no §7 row runs to produce a number `tp audit --merge` already computes over the same files.
suggestion: Cut L130-134. Replace with one sentence in §2.1: the previous cycle's mix is read by running `tp audit --merge` over that cycle's `audit-round-*.ndjson` and reading `by_severity` — an existing command over files already in the tree, no new doc surface and nothing untested. If a SKILL.md sentence is still wanted, it is a cross-reference to `--merge`, not a recipe.

finding: §2.1 places a shipped artifact in `skills/tp/SKILL.md` — "`skills/tp/SKILL.md` carries the one-line command that derives it, next to the field's documentation, so the decision has a stated basis" — and §7 has no row for it. It is not covered by row 19, which edits a different sentence in the same file (§6a.2's convergence-counting claim). Two independent edits to one file, one of them guarded and one not, is exactly the coordination defect §6a warns about for items 1-3, in the same release. Nothing in §7 fails if the command is never added, or is added and does not run.
suggestion: Add a row asserting the command's presence in SKILL.md next to the field's documentation, and — since the section's claim is that the operator gets a number — that running it against the committed projection reproduces §2.1's own per-cycle severity mix.

finding: Round 10 raised this at medium (implementer, `incomplete-write-path-enumeration`); the rewrite did not fix it and made it load-bearing. §3 still closes the set — "The three write paths are `tp set --workflow`, its `--project` form, and `tp import`" — while `tp config --extract` writes BOTH layers for this field: it merges the hoisted value into .tp/config.json (internal/cli/config_extract.go:297-302, mergeCommon + engine.WriteProjectConfig) and then DELETES the field from every task file (line 303-309, engine.StripTaskWorkflowFields(f, fields)). The strip is keyed on the field NAME, so --extract is a second sink that removes the task layer — directly contradicting §3's new sentence "`tp set --project` can only ever write the lower layer, so it cannot uncover anything; **the sink that uncovers is `tp import`**". And §7 row 4 newly REQUIRES the field to be in `hoistedFields` (internal/cli/config_extract.go:108), so this release deliberately wires `audit_converge_on` into the fourth writer in §7 while §3 says there are three. (--extract is in fact resolution-preserving, because it writes the value one layer down before stripping and hoists only fields unanimous across every task file — but §3 makes no such argument, no §7 row asserts it, and `tp config --extract --force` is unfenced under TP_UNATTENDED.)
suggestion: Either enumerate four write paths and state why --extract needs no fence — with a §7 row asserting the resolved value is unchanged across `tp config --extract --force` under TP_UNATTENDED=1, mutant 'hoist without stripping, or strip without hoisting' — or drop the field from §7 row 4's `hoistedFields` requirement and say so.

finding: The escalation route §3 names does not terminate. §3: "the operator's resolution is to write the field explicitly into the imported document." Traced under `tp run`: the imported document is authored by the `decompose` unit itself (engine.UnitDecompose, internal/engine/unitkind.go:25; resumepayload.go:205 'decompose the converged spec into tasks and tp import'), and the decompose predicate is `taskFileHasTasks` (internal/engine/unitkind.go:206) — an import that wrote nothing leaves the task file at zero tasks, so DetectPhase returns `decompose` again. `tp escalate` writes a record and exits 2 and nothing else (internal/cli/escalate.go:91-119: engine.WriteEscalation, then os.Exit(ExitUsage)); there is no answer channel back, and SKILL.md states 'Nothing is replayed'. So after the operator answers and restarts, a fresh decompose unit writes a fresh document and the same import is refused again — the escalation loops. The two resolutions that DO survive a restart are ones §3 does not name: an attended `tp set --workflow audit_converge_on=blocking` at the layer the import will replace, or changing the project layer.
suggestion: Name a resolution that survives the unit re-running: an attended write of the field at the task layer (which makes resolved-before equal resolved-after for every subsequent import), or a change to the project layer. Delete 'write the field explicitly into the imported document', which the next decompose unit overwrites.

finding: The fence's activation vocabulary is pinned at two points and the shipped predicate covers a wider set. §3 says the fence "refuses under `TP_UNATTENDED=1`" and row 12 repeats the literal `=1`; row 13c pins the negative case as "`TP_UNATTENDED` unset". engine.UnattendedActive (internal/engine/unattended.go:27) is on for any present, non-empty value other than `"0"` — `true`, `yes`, `00`, `" "` all activate, and `""` and `"0"` do not, with TestUnattendedActive_ActivationVocabulary pinning that set. A test written from §3 and rows 12/13c alone passes an implementation that compares against the literal `"1"`, which would silently un-fence every harness that writes `true` — the precise case that predicate's comment says it exists for. The spec never says the new fence reuses that predicate.
suggestion: State the fence's activation as "under unattended mode as tp already defines it (`engine.Unattended`)" rather than as the literal `TP_UNATTENDED=1`, and have row 12 or 13c assert one non-`1` activating value and `TP_UNATTENDED=0` as non-activating, so the boundary is asserted rather than assumed.

finding: §3 adds a fifth user-approved decision and a new `--decision` enum member, and the spec budgets for neither the enumerations that go stale nor the exhaustive test loop that will stay green. Measured this session: `internal/cli/escalate.go:41` ships the help string '--decision is one of skip-gate, raise-review-cap, raise-audit-cap, import-force'; `escalate.go:32` ships a parallel prose enumeration; `internal/cli/escalate_test.go:158` loops `[]string{"skip-gate","raise-review-cap","raise-audit-cap","import-force","other"}`, so adding a member without touching that loop leaves the suite green with the new member untested; `skills/tp/SKILL.md:372` says 'the four decisions above stop being available to it' and lists them; and `CLAUDE.md` carries the same 'four user-approved decisions' enumeration twice. §7 row 14 pins only that a fenced refusal *records* `--decision audit-converge-on` and that its message names this field — nothing pins that the closed enum's own enumerations were widened, and nothing pins that the new member is in the validated set. This is the same class as §6a's miss, one section earlier: the release changes a closed set and counts only the sites it thought of. Confirmed by count: the spec names `CLAUDE.md` 0 times and `README.md` 0 times, where the twin release spec/0.31.0.md — shipping the identical knob on the review side — names `CLAUDE.md` 5 times and `README.md` 2 times in its §9 Documentation section. (README itself is genuinely fine here: README.md:206 delegates the workflow field table to REFERENCE.md, so it needs no field row. CLAUDE.md is not fine.)
suggestion: Add to §3: the `--decision` enum's shipped enumerations widen with it — `escalate.go`'s help and prose, `escalate_test.go`'s exhaustive loop, `skills/tp/SKILL.md`'s 'four decisions' paragraph and `CLAUDE.md`'s two. Then either fold them into §6a's rule (preferred, since they are the same class) or give §7 one row: the enum's validated set, its help text and its test loop agree, asserted by deriving the set from one place rather than restating it.

finding: §3 declares the write paths to be three (`tp set --workflow`, its `--project` form, `tp import`) while row 4 makes `tp config --extract` field-aware — a fourth command that writes `audit_converge_on` into `.tp/config.json`. Whether extract needs the fence is never stated. If the fence is built as three per-command patches, which §3's enumeration invites, extract ships unfenced; if it is built at the resolution layer, extract is covered and the enumeration is misleading about the design. The safety argument (extract hoists only a value common to every task file, so nothing it writes can change what resolves for them) is derivable but appears nowhere, so the implementer re-derives it or guesses.
suggestion: State whether the fence is a rule at the resolution layer or a set of per-command checks, and record extract's exemption with its reason — or add it to the fenced list.

finding: §3 says the release 'adds `audit-converge-on` to that enum, maps the field to it, and refuses with a message', which reads as a refusal naming a decision the unit then escalates with; row 14 says 'a fenced refusal **records** `--decision audit-converge-on`'. Those are different builds — the refusing command writing the run's escalation record itself, versus exiting 2 with a message the unit acts on by calling `tp escalate` — and they differ in whether a run reaches `stop_reason: escalation` without the unit cooperating, in what the exit code means, and in what row 14 can observe.
suggestion: Say which actor writes the escalation record, and restate row 14's assertion against that actor's observable.

finding: §3 specifies the fence as a comparison of resolved-before against resolved-after but never says a refused write leaves the tree unchanged. On `tp set` that is harmless; on `tp import`, which replaces the whole task-level workflow block and the task array, resolved-after is knowable only after the document is parsed and the prospective block assembled, so the implementer must decide whether the refusal happens before any bytes are written, after a write plus rollback, or after a partial write. Rows 12 and 13b assert an exit code and nothing about file state, so all three implementations pass.
suggestion: State that a fenced refusal is a no-op — exit 2 before any file is written — and assert it in rows 12 and 13b (the task file and .tp/config.json are byte-identical after the refusal).

finding: §3's escalation paragraph names no value, and one of the two values it could mean is still refused. It says such an import "is an escalation rather than a deadlock" because "the operator's resolution is to write the field explicitly into the imported document". In row 13b's scenario (task-level `all`, project-level `blocking`, imported document carrying a `workflow` key without the field) writing `audit_converge_on: all` preserves the resolved value and passes, while writing `audit_converge_on: blocking` changes the resolved value and is refused by the very change rule §3 states two paragraphs earlier. The paragraph's load-bearing claim — that this refusal differs from the two table deadlocks because a document the unit could write would pass — is therefore true for exactly one literal and the spec does not say which. No §7 row asserts the resolution path at all.
suggestion: Name the literal: state that the resolving document is one carrying `audit_converge_on: all` (or whatever the resolved-before value was), and add a §7 row asserting that this import passes under `TP_UNATTENDED` while the row-13b document is refused. Without a row, the difference between an escalation and a deadlock is untested prose.

finding: Row 19 prescribes the replacement clause for both doc sentences — audit convergence counts every non-`PASS` row 'whose severity the resolved policy treats as blocking'. §2 defines blocking severity as `error` (plus unrecognised) with no policy relativity, and under `all` cleanliness does not consult severity at all: every non-`PASS` row counts whatever its severity. Read with §2's definition the replacement is false under the default (it implies warning and info rows do not count); read as policy-relative it uses 'blocking' in a sense §2 never defines. §6a's closing line claims each replacement is true under both values, so the implementer cannot ship the prescribed literal and satisfy §6a at the same time.
suggestion: Either define in §2 what 'the resolved policy treats as blocking' means under `all` (every severity), or give a replacement sentence that names both policies explicitly.

finding: Row 20 requires REFERENCE.md's 'Honest Convergence Signals' paragraph to stop listing the stored per-round `clean` flag, and its own mutant column concedes that leaving it is something 'the guard does not currently catch'. So the row names an assertion with no enforcing mechanism: the release must extend the docs-contract guard over that paragraph — new work the spec does not describe, with no anchor phrase or literal given — or accept a one-time edit no test protects. §6a items 2 and 3 are explicitly pinned by a named guard and item 4 is not, and the difference is never acknowledged.
suggestion: State what the guard asserts over that paragraph (an anchor phrase, or the absence of the `clean` mention), or mark item 4 as a deliberately unguarded edit and say why that is acceptable.

finding: §6a's heading and framing say five shipped assertions are *reversed*; row 18 requires the eleven `assert.`/`require.` sites in TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate to become nine and the nine to be 'the ones that do not name `audit_converge_on`' — that is deletion. A genuinely reversed assertion (the field IS a known workflow field) keeps the count at eleven and still names the field, failing row 18 on both clauses. The spec never says which is wanted, and under the deletion reading the gate guard ends this release asserting strictly less than it does today, with no row taking over the positive statement.
suggestion: Say explicitly that the two sites are removed, and either add a row asserting the field is now a legal workflow field at that guard, or state why the guard should no longer carry it.

finding: Row 11 depends on a committed projection whose path, schema and derivation the spec never gives — only a size (~295 KiB), a provenance ('committed with the commit it was taken from') and the four fields it keeps. An implementer must invent a location, a row format and a regeneration procedure, and no later reader can check that the fixture is still the projection of the corpus it claims, which is the only thing making row 11's four numbers falsifiable. §7's own paragraph two states that a row depending on a file now states it.
suggestion: Name the fixture path, its per-row schema, the command that regenerates it from spec/.tp-review/, and how the source commit is recorded so a drifted fixture is detectable.

finding: Row 9b names no surface, and the one it would inherit cannot see its mutant. Row 9 pins `state.json` explicitly ("the only surface carrying more than the latest round"); row 9b opens with "and the relaxing direction" and names no read path, so an implementer either inherits `state.json` — where the named mutant, "add a read-side floor that re-blocks it", changes nothing, since a read-side floor by definition does not rewrite the store — or picks a payload the spec never named. Two engineers write two different tests, and one of them cannot fail. §7's own new rule for this round is that a row depending on a file or a function states it.
suggestion: Name 9b's surface, and make it a read surface: `tp audit --status` after the knob returns to `all` reports `consecutive_clean` counting the round recorded under `blocking`. That is the value a read-side floor moves.

finding: §7 rows 19 and 20 are the release's two doc reversals, and neither can be verified by the mechanism the rows name. Row 19 says the two sentences are "asserted by the docs-contract guard's two independent checks". Read this session: internal/cli/docs_contract_test.go:96 defines `divergenceCountingSubstring = "audit convergence still counts every non-PASS row"` and :132 asserts `Contains(skill, ...)`. That is a 46-character SUBSTRING of skills/tp/SKILL.md:149, and the sentence it sits in continues "...the stored per-round `clean` flag, `next_action` and the `--status --check` exit code are unchanged: audit convergence still counts every non-PASS row, so `--check` still exits 1 and `next_action` still reads fix-and-re-audit." Perform row 19's edit exactly as written -- qualify the counting clause -- and the guard goes green while the same sentence still promises three unchanged things this release changes and one `next_action` branch it replaces. The guard cannot catch that, by construction: it pins a substring, so it is blind to every clause around it. Row 20 states the same problem in its own mutant column: "leave it, which the guard does not currently catch". A column whose contract is "the mutant that must fail it" cannot be satisfied by a mutant nothing fails, and §7's own new rule this round -- "A test whose subject the spec cannot name is a decision that has not been made yet" -- is the rule row 20 breaks. Row 21 has the third variant: "its comment no longer calls condition 4 redundant" is an assertion over a Go doc comment, and no guard in this repository asserts a Go doc comment (the docs-contract guard reads markdown via `readRepoDoc` plus one exported constant).
suggestion: For row 19, change the unit of repair from the clause to the sentence, and change the guard's literal with it: replace `divergenceCountingSubstring` with the whole rewritten SKILL.md sentence, so the guard fails until every clause is true under both values. For row 20, name the guard extension the row requires -- a new pinned sentence for REFERENCE.md's Honest Convergence Signals paragraph in `referenceSignalSentences` -- and rewrite the mutant as "leave the paragraph, which the extended guard fails"; a row whose mutant nothing catches is not a test. For row 21, drop the comment half of the assertion or state the mechanism (there is none today); the behavioural half stands on its own.

finding: §2 requires that invalid values are refused "on the same terms and with the same hint as `review_converge_on`", and no row asserts the hint. Row 3 asserts exit codes only (`ExitUsage` at the write sink, `ExitValidation` at the consuming sink). Hint parity is the half an agent actually consumes — it is what names the two legal literals — and it is the half that silently drifts, since nothing compares the two fields' messages.
suggestion: Extend row 3 or add a row: the refusal message for an invalid `audit_converge_on` names both legal values and matches `review_converge_on`'s hint shape, asserted by comparing the two commands' stderr rather than by a literal copied into the test.

finding: §2 says an invalid value is refused at 'the consuming sink' and row 3 names only `tp audit --record` and `--status`. The other readers of the resolved workflow are unaddressed: the plain prompt-emitting `tp audit <spec>`, which prints the loop budget; `tp resume` / `tp run`'s oracle; and `tp config --resolved`. The implementer must decide whether those refuse, ignore the value, or fall back to `all` — and a silent fallback at one reader while another exits ExitValidation gives two answers about the same stored file, which is the failure mode fail-closed grading exists to avoid.
suggestion: Name every reader that validates, or state a single resolution point that validates once so all readers inherit the refusal.

finding: §2.1 makes a documented one-line command a deliverable — the command deriving the previous cycle's severity mix from `audit-round-*.ndjson`, which §2.1 calls the stated basis for the whole decision — without giving the command, the directory it runs over, or what it prints. §7 carries no row for it, so the single artifact §2.1 says an operator needs at decision time is both unspecified and unverified, while §7 claims every row derives from a numbered decision.
suggestion: Give the command verbatim in §2.1 and add a §7 row asserting SKILL.md carries it beside the field's documentation.

finding: Round 10 raised this (regression, `sink-reads-wrong-layer`); the rewrite dropped the phrase 'at every sink' but kept the rule and left the gap. §3 says the change rule "compares resolved-before against resolved-after" and names `tp import` as the uncovering sink, without saying which task file the import sink resolves against. The one reusable helper resolves the wrong one: `resolvedWorkflowForFence()` (internal/cli/unattended.go:90-98) resolves whatever `engine.DiscoverTaskFile(".", flagFile)` returns — the --file/TP_FILE/.tp/local.json active pointer — while `tp import` writes `targetPath` derived from the imported document's own `tf.Spec` (internal/cli/importcmd.go:141-143). Whenever the active pointer is not the import's target, the fence compares a file the write does not touch, and both false-refuse and false-pass are reachable.
suggestion: State that each sink resolves the file it is about to write: `tp set --workflow` the discovered task file, `tp set --project` the project config under that same file, `tp import` the target derived from the document's `spec` field. Add it to §7 row 12 as an assertion with an active pointer deliberately pointed at a different spec.

finding: §3 scopes the fence to `TP_UNATTENDED=1` and row 13c tests the variable unset; everything in between is unspecified — `TP_UNATTENDED=0`, `TP_UNATTENDED=true`, or set-but-empty. An implementer choosing `value == "1"` and one choosing 'set and non-empty' both satisfy §3 and row 13c while disagreeing about whether the fence applies, and the disagreement runs in the unsafe direction for any runner that exports a different truthy value.
suggestion: State the predicate once — which values count as unattended — and have row 13c assert the boundary rather than only the unset case.

finding: §3 tells the implementer what to copy and the named model cannot carry the rule. "The string-shaped fence tp already runs — placed before the type dispatch — is what to copy." The only string-shaped fence tp runs is `engine.FencedCommandField` (internal/engine/unattended.go:66-68), called at internal/cli/set.go:361, set_project.go:46 and set_local.go:41. It is value- and layer-INDEPENDENT: it refuses `runner`/`notify_cmd` at any value and any layer, reads no resolved value, and so supplies no comparison at all. The only code that compares a requested value against a resolved one is `fenceWorkflowWrite` (unattended.go:56-76) — the numeric fence §3 explicitly rules out two sentences earlier. Copied as instructed, the model yields a FIELD-scoped fence, which is the first rule §3's own table rejects as deadlocking Workflow A step 6.
suggestion: Say that the fence borrows the PLACEMENT from the command-field check (before the type dispatch, so a string field is reached) and the RESOLVED COMPARISON from `fenceWorkflowWrite`, rather than naming either as the thing to copy.

finding: §3's three-row rejected-rules table (L156-170, 1,289 bytes counted this session) is already carried by §7's mutant column, so the release states the same three failures twice and a decomposer reads both. Row 13's mutant is 'a field-scoped or value-scoped fence, both of which refuse the third and deadlock Workflow A step 6' — that is table rows 1 and 2. Row 13b's mutant is 'build the fence from the three shapes in §3's table, which do not reach this input' — that is table row 3's shape plus the uncovering case. The mutant column is the better home for the reasoning, because a mutant is checked by running while a table of rejected designs is checked by reading, which is the substitution the file's own header paragraph says this rewrite was about.
suggestion: Cut the table and its lead-in (L158-165), keep the normative sentence 'The fence refuses a write that CHANGES the resolved value to `blocking` — not the field, not the value, not a transition between literals', and keep the paragraph after it that says why the change rule answers all three. Reword row 13b's mutant so it no longer references the deleted table: 'a fence scoped to the field, to the value, or to an `all` to `blocking` transition — none of which reaches an import naming neither literal'. Returns ~1,100 bytes and removes a drift pair.

finding: The revert to '≥1 non-`PASS` row' is correct and well argued, but it deleted the only stated ground for the `--compact` half and did not replace it. Round 10's text justified survival as 'it survives `--compact` *because* its mere presence then signals the accepted-open state' — true only while the key was gated on cleanliness. Under the new condition the key is present on every round that holds any finding, so its presence signals nothing, and `--compact`'s whole job is stripping what is not decision-bearing. §4 now asserts 'and it survives `--compact`' with no reason, and §7 row 16 still pins it with the mutant 'strip it as explanatory' — which is exactly the reading the section no longer refutes.
suggestion: Give the retention its own ground under the new condition — e.g. that the breakdown is the only surface separating the round's blocking rows from its advisory ones, so a compacted payload without it cannot answer why a round was clean — or drop the --compact clause and row 16.

finding: This prices the cost of the round-10 revert, which I asked for and did not price. The reverted predicate is right — a breakdown of the rows in front of it needs no policy — but it makes an opt-in feature's output unconditional. Measured this session: 70 of 90 tracked `audit-round-*.ndjson` files (78%) carry at least one non-`PASS` row, and the resolved default is `all`, which no project in this repository's corpus has ever overridden. Under `all` the map feeds no decision the payload does not already carry: a round is unclean iff any non-`PASS` row exists, which `findings` and `by_status` state, and the severity mix changes nothing about the verdict. So `by_severity` is emitted on ~78% of `tp audit --merge` invocations to serve the operators who have set `blocking` plus the once-a-cycle default decision §2.1 describes. §4 then adds 'and it survives `--compact`', which is where a byte an agent does not need is supposed to be stripped — and `overlap_report`, the only other map on this payload, IS stripped under `--compact` as explanatory. The map is worth emitting; it is not worth emitting in the payload whose entire purpose is that an agent asked for less.
suggestion: Reverse the `--compact` clause: `by_severity` is emitted whenever the round holds a non-`PASS` row and is stripped under `--compact`, like `overlap_report`. Change §7 row 16 to assert the strip, with the mutant 'keep it under `--compact`, which bills every default-policy round for a breakdown its verdict does not read'. An operator making §2.1's decision is not running `--compact`.

finding: `tp audit --merge` deduplicates rows and reports `duplicates_removed`; §4 says the new counter goes in the loop that builds `by_status` and `by_role` but never says whether `by_severity` counts the deduplicated set or the raw inputs. Row 17 ties `error` + `unrecognised` to 'the round's blocking-row count', which is the deduplicated population only if the counter runs after dedup — under the other reading a duplicated `error` row inflates the blocking count that §2's fail-closed rule is supposed to mirror.
suggestion: State that `by_severity` counts the merged (deduplicated) rows, the same population as `by_status`, and say so in row 17's assertion.

finding: §4 says every row lands in a named bucket but never says whether `by_severity` always carries all four keys (zeros included) or only the buckets that are non-empty. The two counters it is explicitly modelled on, `by_status` and `by_role`, carry only observed keys, so the natural implementation omits `error` on an advisory-only round — exactly the round §4 exists for. Row 17's invariant is written as a sum over keys that may then be absent, and an agent reading `by_severity.error` to decide whether the round blocks must know whether absent means zero or means unknown.
suggestion: State that all four keys are present with explicit zeros whenever the object is emitted (or that absent means zero), and assert that in row 17.

finding: §4 states the emission condition as "Emitted when the round holds at least one non-`PASS` row" and row 15 asserts the biconditional, including "**absent** on an all-`PASS` round". "Emitted when X" does not by itself forbid emission when not-X, and the section's other governing sentence — "Every row lands in a named bucket, because the point is that nothing hides" — reads naturally as an argument for emitting `{}` rather than omitting the key. An implementer reading §4 and an implementer reading row 15 write different code, and only one of them is caught.
suggestion: Write §4's condition as an iff — "present exactly when the round holds at least one non-`PASS` row; absent, not empty, otherwise" — since row 15 already depends on the exclusive reading.

finding: Non-Goal 6 — "`AuditRowIsPass` stays byte-exact on `status == \"PASS\"`" — is a preservation claim about this release and appears neither as a §7 row nor in §7's deliberate-absence paragraph, which names only the three streak surfaces. Every other numbered Non-Goal either defers to `spec/0.46.0.md` (2, 3, 4), restates a role-scoping deferral (1) or is about review (5); 6 is the only one asserting that this release's own predicate is unchanged, and this release adds a second grading step immediately beside it. §7's opening rule is that every row derives from a numbered decision; the converse — a numbered decision with no row and no stated absence — is unhandled here.
suggestion: Either add a row (a padded `" PASS"` row is non-`PASS` under both values of the field, so the severity grading runs strictly after the status predicate) or name Non-Goal 6 in the deliberate-absence paragraph with the existing guard that covers it.

finding: §6a item 1 and §7 row 18 pin a count of test-internal call sites and then pin the counting rule that produces it: 'Two of the eleven `assert.`/`require.` call sites in `TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate` (`internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go`); the other nine stand — nine under that counting rule, which includes two `require.True(t, ok)` decode checks, and the rule is stated because without it the number is 7.' Row 18 then asserts eleven becomes nine. Nothing here is establishable except against code, and the numbers move on any unrelated edit to that test — adding one decode check to an assertion the release does not touch turns 11 into 12 and reddens a row that is measuring nothing about this release. This is the canonical `over-specification` smell: the spec is prescribing a mechanism whose correctness only the tree can establish, in the section a decomposer reads to size the work. The behaviour that matters is stateable without a number.
suggestion: §6a item 1: 'the gate guard's assertion that `audit_converge_on` is an unknown workflow field is removed; every other assertion in that test stands.' §7 row 18: 'after the change, `TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate` contains no assertion naming `audit_converge_on`, and the assertions that do not name it are unchanged — mutant: delete the surrounding block, which also removes assertions the release does not reverse.' That is checkable by running, needs no counting rule, and does not rot.

finding: §6a's new framing asserts two things it does not tie to an artifact. (1) "The list is exhaustive over what `git grep` finds today; a sixth would be a defect in this section, not a surprise." No grep is named, no pattern is given, and no §7 row asserts the set is complete — rows 18-21 each check one member. This is the count that has already been wrong three times (one, two, three, now five), stated again as prose rather than as a runnable derivation. (2) "Both additions were found by walking the call graph out of `clean` rather than by searching for the sentence" is false for item 4: `REFERENCE.md`'s 'Honest Convergence Signals' paragraph is markdown prose, reachable by no call graph, and round 10's architect finding cites it as a document reference alongside the divergence comment. Item 1's counting rule, by contrast, verifies exactly: `TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate` (internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go:469-503) holds eleven assert./require. call sites, two naming `audit_converge_on` (lines 473-474), nine surviving including two `require.True(t, ok)` decode checks (493, 497) — 7 without them, as stated.
suggestion: Replace the exhaustiveness sentence with the derivation: give the literal grep whose hit set is the five items, and add a §7 row asserting that grep returns nothing outside them after the edits. Fix the provenance sentence — one addition came from the call graph out of `clean` (item 5), the other from reading the document the guard pins (item 4).

finding: Half of row 2 is a tautology no implementation can fail. The row asserts that "a `TP_AUDIT_CONVERGE_ON` in the environment and an `--audit-converge-on` flag both change nothing", with the mutant "add either layer to `engine.ResolveWorkflowLayers`". Verified: that function (internal/engine/configresolve.go:233) takes exactly two `*model.WorkflowOverride` arguments, so adding an env layer to it does make the environment half fail — but no change to it can create a CLI flag, and a command invoked with an unregistered `--audit-converge-on` fails at flag parsing, which also "changes nothing". The flag half therefore passes both on correct code and on the named mutant, for two different reasons.
